outputs.L2: A method includes causing a vibration mode in a flow tube (130, 130′) to be excited. outputs.L3:
A vibration mode of a flow tube is excited by means of first and second drivers coupled to the flow tube. The two drivers are driven with amplitude-modulated drive signals that are out of phase with one another, so that the applied excitation produces a controlled modal response of the tube.

The drive command supplied to the first and second drivers is formed as a composite signal. In particular, the drive command comprises a sum of \(N+1\) independent signals, allowing the drivers to be excited simultaneously or sequentially at a plurality of distinct frequency components. These frequency components include multiple off-resonance frequencies selected near, but not exactly at, a resonant drive frequency associated with the vibration mode of interest.

By exciting the drivers at the multiple off-resonance frequencies, the system can observe the resulting modal response of the flow tube under known excitation conditions. For each off-resonance frequency, the effective phase relationship between the modal response and the excitation applied by the drivers is inferred. This phase relationship provides information about how the flow tube responds dynamically to the applied drive forces away from resonance.

For each of the off-resonance excitation frequencies, a left eigenvector phase estimate is generated. The collection of left eigenvector phase estimates is then used to estimate the left eigenvector phase corresponding to the resonant drive frequency. In this way, the system can determine or approximate the modal phase behavior at resonance without relying solely on measurements taken exactly at the resonant frequency.

In addition, the method measures the phase difference between signals generated by first and second pickoffs associated with the flow tube. This measured pickoff phase is used to determine a right eigenvector phase for the flow tube. Together, the estimated left eigenvector phase and the measured right eigenvector phase characterize the modal behavior of the flow tube and may be used to improve drive control, modal identification, or flow tube measurement accuracy.
outputs.L4:
A method is provided for characterizing the vibrational behavior of a flow tube, such as a flow tube used in a Coriolis flowmeter or similar vibrating conduit device. The method includes exciting a selected vibration mode of the flow tube by applying drive forces to the tube using two or more drivers. The drivers are operated with relative phases selected to produce an out-of-phase excitation pattern, thereby preferentially exciting the desired vibration mode.

Rather than driving the flow tube only at or near its resonance frequency, the drivers are supplied with a composite drive signal formed from a sum of multiple independent signals. Each independent signal has a different frequency, and the selected frequencies are positioned away from the resonance frequency of the vibration mode being characterized. These off-resonance excitation frequencies allow the modal response of the flow tube to be observed under conditions in which the response is less dominated by resonance effects and can therefore provide useful information about the phase behavior of the system.

The vibration response of the flow tube is measured using one or more motion sensors or pickoffs coupled to the tube. For each of the off-resonance excitation frequencies, the measured response is analyzed to determine modal response phases. The relationship between the applied driver signals and the measured motion responses is then used to estimate phases associated with a left eigenvector of the vibration mode. In this context, the left eigenvector represents how the applied drive forces couple into the modal dynamics of the flow tube, while the corresponding phase information describes the phase relationship between the excitation forces and the modal response.

The left eigenvector phase estimates obtained at the multiple off-resonance frequencies are then used to estimate the left eigenvector phase at the resonance frequency of the selected vibration mode. This may be accomplished by fitting, interpolating, extrapolating, or otherwise processing the off-resonance phase estimates to determine the expected phase value at resonance. Because the estimate is based on measurements taken at several independent frequencies, the resulting resonant phase estimate can be more robust than an estimate based on a single frequency measurement.

In addition to estimating the left eigenvector phase, the method also determines a right eigenvector phase of the vibration mode. The right eigenvector characterizes the spatial pattern of motion of the flow tube for the selected mode. This phase is determined from phase measurements obtained from the pickoffs, which sense the motion of the vibrating tube at different locations. By comparing the phases of the pickoff signals, the method identifies the phase relationship between different portions of the tube and thereby estimates the right eigenvector phase.

Together, the estimated left eigenvector phase at resonance and the pickoff-derived right eigenvector phase provide a more complete characterization of the selected vibration mode of the flow tube. This improved modal characterization can be used to enhance calibration, diagnostics, compensation, or control of the vibrating flow tube. In particular, the method can improve the accuracy with which modal properties are identified, reduce sensitivity to measurement noise or resonant distortion, and support more precise operation of flow measurement systems that rely on controlled vibration of the flow tube.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. As a definite article, “the” helps identify a specific person, place, object, or idea. For example, when someone says “the book,” they are not talking about just any book—they mean a particular one.

This simple word adds clarity and precision to sentences. It helps listeners and readers understand exactly what is being discussed. Without “the,” English would feel less natural and often less clear. Phrases like “the sun,” “the world,” and “the future” show how the word can point to something unique, familiar, or important.

Although “the” may seem ordinary, it is essential in everyday speech and writing. It connects ideas, gives meaning to nouns, and helps structure language. In many ways, “the” proves that even the smallest words can have a big impact.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise patent abstract describing a method where first and second drivers on a flow tube are driven by a sum of N+1 independent signals to infer modal response phase at off-resonance frequencies and estimate eigenvector phase at resonance.
counterfactuals.output: A method for characterizing vibration of a flow tube includes applying drive signals to first and second drivers coupled to the flow tube, each driver being driven by a respective sum of N+1 independent excitation signals. The excitation signals include components selected to excite a vibratory mode at a plurality of off-resonance frequencies. Motion of the flow tube is sensed in response to the applied drive signals, and modal response phases associated with the off-resonance frequencies are determined from the sensed motion and the independent excitation signals. The determined modal response phases are processed to estimate an eigenvector phase corresponding to the vibratory mode at resonance. The estimated eigenvector phase may be used to calibrate, compensate, or operate a vibratory flowmeter, including correcting phase-related measurement errors in a Coriolis flowmeter.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical patent paragraph for a vibrating flow tube system with drivers 180L and 180R and pickoffs 170L and 170R, including off-resonance excitation, left eigenvector phase estimation, and right eigenvector determination.
counterfactuals.output: In one embodiment, a vibrating flow tube system includes at least one flow tube configured to receive a process fluid, a pair of vibration drivers 180L and 180R operatively coupled to the flow tube at spaced-apart locations, and a pair of motion pickoffs 170L and 170R positioned to generate respective sensor signals indicative of tube motion. A controller is configured to energize one or both of the drivers 180L and 180R with an excitation signal selected to drive the flow tube at an off-resonance frequency, whereby a forced vibration response is produced without requiring operation at a natural resonant frequency of the tube. The controller receives the pickoff signals from pickoffs 170L and 170R and processes the signals to estimate phase, amplitude, and modal response characteristics of the vibrating tube. In particular, the controller may determine a left eigenvector associated with the measured system response, the left eigenvector being used to estimate a phase relationship between the pickoff signals and/or between the excitation and response signals under off-resonance operating conditions. Based at least in part on the estimated left eigenvector phase information, the controller further determines a corresponding right eigenvector representative of a vibration mode shape of the flow tube, including relative displacement, velocity, or phase components at the driver and pickoff locations. The determined right eigenvector may be used to compensate for drive imbalance, pickoff gain variation, damping asymmetry, fluid loading, or structural perturbations, thereby enabling improved determination of flow-related parameters such as mass flow rate, density, tube stiffness, or diagnostic condition while the flow tube is excited at a frequency offset from resonance.
